titulo: PPO with thousands of robots in parallel
lead: The algorithm that trains almost every humanoid gait today is PPO, running thousands of copies of the robot on the GPU. In this lesson you learn the collect, estimate, and update loop, run a ~120-line PPO with mjlab's values on CPU, with 16 robots, and see the command that does the same with 4,096.
objetivo: run a short PPO training on CPU that saves a checkpoint and a log, and read the values from a real training run in mjlab.

aprende.t: The loop: collect 24 steps per robot, estimate the advantage, update the network
The G1's hyperparameters in mjlab: lr 1e-3 adaptive, clip 0.2, 5 epochs
20 iterations on CPU: checkpoint and progresso.csv
At scale (shown): 4,096 environments on the GPU, 30,000 iterations

hero_alt: Monitor in a dark room showing dozens of small, identical humanoid robots walking in simulation, arranged in a grid.

secoes.sub: Click each block. Training repeats this loop thousands of times.

nos.detalhe: Each environment runs 24 steps (num_steps_per_env) with the current policy, which samples the action around the mean (exploration). With 16 environments, that's 384 samples; with 4,096, it's 98,304 per iteration.
The critic estimates how much each state is worth. The advantage (GAE, with gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95) tells you whether an action was better or worse than expected.
5 epochs over the data, in 4 mini-batches. The "clip" (clip 0.2) keeps the new policy from drifting too far from the one that collected the data: this is what gives PPO its stability.
The learning rate starts at 1e-3 and adjusts itself: it goes down if the policy changed more than the divergence target (desired_kl 0.01), and goes up if it changed less.
At the end, the kit writes the weights (modelo_N.pt) and one line per iteration to progresso.csv, with the reward and each term. mjlab saves every 50 iterations.

secoes.legenda: Actor and critic network: 512-256-128 with ELU, normalized observations, as in mjlab for the G1.

secoes.sub: kit/ppo.py uses the names and defaults from the G1's rl_cfg.py in mjlab (commit 8bb2bc9, 10/18/2026; rsl-rl-lib library 5.5.1).

blocos.conteudo:
PADRAO = dict(clip_param=0.2, entropy_coef=0.01, value_loss_coef=1.0, num_learning_epochs=5,
              num_mini_batches=4, learning_rate=1.0e-3, desired_kl=0.01, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95,
              max_grad_norm=1.0, num_steps_per_env=24, init_std=1.0, hidden_dims=(512, 256, 128))

secoes.sub: 16 G1s in parallel in MuJoCo, one core, with the reward from lesson 4. The 900 s cap is a safety margin: here it took seconds.

Check the format, not the value: 20 it lines, checkpoint salvo:, the file exists, and progresso.csv has 21 lines (header + 20). The negative average reward and the falls show that 20 iterations don't teach the G1 to walk; mjlab uses max_iterations=30_000. The total time changes from one machine to another.

Three current paths, all on the GPU. Click each one.

texto: Isaac Lab's "manager-based" API on top of MuJoCo Warp 3.16, Apache-2.0, with uv. It requires an NVIDIA GPU (on macOS, evaluation only). It is the closest relative of this kit: the same term names.

unitree_rl_lab, BeyondMimic and Berkeley Humanoid Lite train on Isaac Lab 2.x (pin the version each README indicates). Isaac Lab 3.0 is in early access (EA, 09/16/2026), requires Isaac Sim 6.1 and a new Python 3.12 environment with uv.

(reported) According to the Isaac Lab benchmark table cited in robotica-real2sim, Isaac Lab's own G1 rough-terrain velocity task, with 4,096 environments, runs about 82 thousand steps/s on an RTX 4090 in 3.0 beta; the number varies with the version.
MuJoCo Playground has the G1JoystickFlatTerrain task, with Python 3.12 + uv, on JAX/MJX; training with MJWarp was announced in beta.
legged_gym, on top of Isaac Gym (2021), showed that you can train a gait in minutes with thousands of environments. Today it is legacy: the repositories checked by the course use Isaac Lab or mjlab.

exercicios.pronto: you wrote 98,304 samples per iteration and about 2.9 billion in the full training (384 × 20 = 7,680 in yours: about 384 thousand times more).

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: What does the clip (clip 0.2) do in PPO?
opcoes: It cuts rewards above 0.2 so training doesn't blow up in the first iterations.
It keeps the new policy from drifting too far from the one that collected the data.
It discards 20% of the environments that fell at the start of the episode.
It limits the action to ±0.2 rad around the default pose.
perguntas.explica: The data was collected with the old policy; if the new one changes too much, the data stops being valid. The clip holds the step back, together with the KL-based rate adjustment.

perguntas.p: The 20-iteration training ended with a negative reward. How do you know whether it "worked"?
opcoes: By the format: checkpoint saved, 20 lines in the log, exit 0.
By the final reward, which has to be above zero.
By the total time, which has to be under 10 seconds.
By the number of falls, which has to reach zero in the last iteration.
perguntas.explica: On CPU and with 20 iterations, what you check is the loop. The reward value depends on the machine, the seed, and the duration; the format does not.

perguntas.p: Why doesn't the course actually run mjlab or Isaac Lab?
opcoes: Because mjlab only accepts quadruped robots, not the G1.
Because Isaac Lab doesn't have the G1 velocity task.
Because the kit's PPO is a different algorithm from the one used in those GPU projects.
Because they require an NVIDIA GPU and their own environment, and the course runs on CPU.
perguntas.explica: The values and the names are the same; the scale changes. If you have a GPU, you run the shown commands in a separate environment, with the version pinned.

itens.texto: Collect 24 steps per robot, estimate the advantage with GAE, update with clipping and an adaptive rate.
20 iterations on CPU write a checkpoint and a log; you check the format, not the value.
mjlab uses the same values with 4,096 robots on the GPU and 30,000 iterations.
